newsitem.title: USA: Benefits should be integral to any small business.
newsitem.headline: Benefits should be integral to any small business.

text.p: Setting up a new business can be arduous enough without having to think about issues like pensions and medical insurance, but knowing how to navigate these waters should be integral to any new business.
It's an especially crucial issue for those working at home, who often end up researching every aspect of their business and need to become jack-of-all-trades specialists.

While it's impossible to lay out a single benefits plan for everyone, you should think about what you need and research what is available. An expert, such as an accountant or a pension expert, could help you navigate the waters.

John Ohrnberger, senior manager for compensations benefits at consultants Arthur Anderson, says there are three key areas that self-employed people or business owners should consider: retirement plans, health and disability insurance, and life insurance.

-- Retirement. President Clinton recently signed a law that extends and simplifies 401(k) plans for small businesses and got a lot of attention in the media. That doesn't mean this plan is the best for you.

The plan, which is designed for companies with 100 or fewer employees, allows workers to make up to $6,000 in contributions with a matching contribution from employers. But "it doesn't really make sense for a self-employed person," said Ohrnberger.
Instead, he usually recommends a Simplified Employee Pension plan, or SEP, which allows someone working for themselves to put aside zero percent to 15 percent of their compensation into the plan.

The advantages are that the contribution is not limited to $6,000 and the amount you set aside is flexible. So, if cash flow is tight one year, you have the latitude to set aside less than the maximum.

These plans are also advantageous for someone working full-time who has a pension, but who moonlights as a self-employed person. While a person with a pension plan is limited in taking a tax deduction on an Individual Retirement Account, that isn't the case with a SEP. You can set up a SEP for your separate business and make tax-deductible contributions because each retirement plan is independent of the other.

-- Medical insurance. Ohrnberger said it's "crazy" to work for yourself and not consider health insurance. While the cost of insurance can be prohibitive, he suggests cash-strapped entrepreneurs at least look into catastrophic coverage.

He also points out that under new legislation signed by Clinton the tax deduction for self-employed people on medical insurance is going up -- to 40 percent next year from 30 percent in 1996 and rising steadily to 80 percent by 2006.

Another possibility to consider under the new laws are Medical Savings Accounts. Although these are only a test programme limited to 750,000 taxpayers on a first-come-first-serve basis, they are attractive.

They allow small employers (less than 50 workers) or the self-employed to make tax-deductible contributions to a medical account to pay for expenses not covered in a medical plan. They only apply, however, to plans with high deductibles.

For example, an individual facing a deductible of $2,000 on their health insurance can deposit 65 percent of that money into a tax deductible account. That money can then be used to pay medical expenses. If the money is not used, it can earn interest tax-free. There are no "use-it-or-lose-it" provisions that apply to other medical spending accounts.
The accounts are similar to IRAs. Distributions not used for medical expenses are considered income and subject to an additional 15 percent tax unless withdrawn after age 65, death or disability.

As for disability insurance, Ohrnberger advises to look into a plan that pays out a benefit if you are prevented from working at your own occupation. He also says that accounts in which payments are made with after-tax dollars are usually more advantageous since the benefit is then received tax-free.

-- Life insurance. There are myriad life insurance plans from simple term insurance plans renewable each year, which are the least expensive, to cash value plans that can cost thousands per year -- again it depends on your specific situation.

But there is one type of account to consider if you are in partnership with someone else. Called a buy-sell arrangement, the life insurance provides money to buy out the heirs of a partner if the partner dies or is disabled. "That way the heirs don't have to run the business with you, they can cash out," Ohrnberger said.
